newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: MBOWENI SAYS PARLIAMENT NO HELP TO S.AFRICA LABOUR.
newsitem.headline: MBOWENI SAYS PARLIAMENT NO HELP TO S.AFRICA LABOUR.

text.p: Labour Minister Tito Mboweni on Tuesday cautioned the 1.9-million strong Congress of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu) he would not allow it to press MPs into a no-win situation over planned employment legislation.
"We are now entering injury time in negotiations...," he told the Pretoria Press Club.
"I'm insisting on agreement and won't have our comrades (labour) going to parliament to place unnecessary pressure on ANC parliamentarians by forcing them to take sides."
Cosatu is in an alliance with the ruling African National Congress (ANC), stemming from the apartheid struggle.
Since it came to power in the first all-race polls in 1994, the ANC government has confounded its critics by pursuing market-friendly policies.

But although the government's commitment to a free market and privatisation has wooed foreign investors and South Africa's still predominantly white business community, it has provoked argument with its labour ally.

However, Mboweni was positive that at least sufficient consensus -- if not general agreement -- would be reached between government, business and labour at the statutory Nedlac negotiation forum by the deadline of August 15.
"There is only one way to resolve the issue of the Basic Conditions of Employment Bill and that is through negotiations."
Cosatu upped the ante over the proposed law with a one-day national strike on June 2 and a one-hour stoppage nationwide on Monday this week.

It has also threatened 24-hour strikes in all the major regions from August 18-21 to drive home its core demands: six months' maternity leave, of which four should be paid, and a 40-hour working week to be phased in over five years.
Business is worried about the bill's wide scope and provisions which it says could raise employment costs to the point of creating obstacles to new jobs.
The proposed legislation is scheduled to be presented to parliament for approval on September 15. Mboweni warned the bill was unlikely to become law this year if this date was not met.
